title: Organs of the digestive system

basics: Think of the digestive system as one long tube running through the body with a set of glands hanging off it. Food travels down the tube (the gastrointestinal or GI tract, also called the digestive canal) and never actually enters the body's tissues until its molecules cross the tube's lining. The glands and other helpers that are not part of the tube itself are the accessory organs: teeth and tongue break food up physically; the salivary glands, liver, gallbladder and pancreas pour secretions into the tube through ducts. The slide reproduces Tortora Figure 24.1; every label on it is either a segment of the tube (mouth, pharynx, oesophagus, stomach, duodenum, jejunum, ileum, caecum, colon, rectum, anal canal) or an accessory organ (salivary glands, liver, gallbladder, pancreas). The slide assumes you know the tube is continuous from mouth to anus and that the small intestine has three named parts.

basics: Everything the digestive system does can be filed under six verbs, and the slide is copied almost word for word from the box in Tortora Figure 24.1. Ingestion is getting food into the tube. Secretion is the wall and glands adding roughly seven litres a day of water, acid, buffers and enzymes to the contents. Mixing and propulsion (the book's term is motility) is smooth muscle in the wall churning and moving the contents. Digestion is breaking food into molecules small enough to cross the lining: mechanically by teeth and churning, chemically by enzymes that hydrolyse large molecules. Absorption is the transfer of those small molecules across the lining into blood or lymph. Defecation is expelling what was never absorbed. Unsaid on the slide: a few things (water, ions, vitamins, cholesterol) are absorbed without any digestion, and these six processes overlap in time and place.

basics: Food arrives as lumps of large polymers (starch, proteins, fats, nucleic acids) that cannot cross a cell membrane. Two different things have to happen. Mechanical digestion is purely physical: teeth cut and grind, the stomach and intestine churn, so the lumps become small particles with a huge surface area, dissolved and mixed with the fluids. No chemical bonds are broken. Chemical digestion is bond-breaking: enzymes catalyse hydrolysis, inserting water across the links of a polymer to release monomers (glucose, amino acids, fatty acids, nucleotides). The two are coupled because enzymes only work on molecules they can reach, so mechanical breakdown is what gives the enzymes access. The slide does not say that each enzyme is specific to one class of bond, that the enzymes come from the salivary glands, tongue, stomach, pancreas and intestinal lining, or that each works best at its own pH.

basics: The gut is a tube, and a tube's wall can be described by its layers from the inside out. Innermost, facing the food, is the mucosa: a sheet of epithelial cells (some secreting mucus, some hormones), a thin connective-tissue bed (lamina propria) and a thin muscle film. Next is the submucosa, connective tissue carrying the big blood and lymph vessels and a nerve network (submucosal plexus). Then the thick muscle coat, usually an inner circular ring and an outer longitudinal sheet with the myenteric nerve plexus between them; contraction of these moves and mixes the contents. Outermost is a serous membrane (serosa) where the tube lies free in the abdomen. The slide's figure is not Tortora's drawing but labels the same layers plus the cell types in the epithelium (mucous, exocrine, enteroendocrine) and ducts from outside glands. Unsaid: the exact epithelium changes along the tube (stratified squamous where abrasion is high, simple columnar where absorption happens).

basics: This slide is the text version of the previous figure. The epithelium is the working surface: it protects, secretes and absorbs, and because it is exposed to acid, enzymes and abrasion its cells are replaced every 5-7 days and sealed to each other by tight junctions so nothing leaks between them. The lamina propria beneath is where absorbed nutrients first meet blood and lymph capillaries, and it houses most of the gut's immune tissue (MALT). The muscularis mucosae is a thin muscle film that throws the lining into small folds. The submucosa binds mucosa to muscle coat and carries the larger vessels. The muscular layer's two sheets, circular inside and longitudinal outside, produce the tube's movements; between them lies the myenteric plexus. The serosa is a serous membrane and is literally the same sheet as the visceral peritoneum. Unsaid: mouth, pharynx, upper oesophagus and external anal sphincter have skeletal muscle instead, and the oesophagus has an adventitia, not a serosa.

basics: The gut wall contains its own complete nervous system, the enteric nervous system (ENS), with about as many neurons as the spinal cord. It is arranged as two networks: the myenteric plexus between the two muscle sheets, which mainly governs how hard and how often the muscle contracts, and the submucosal plexus, which mainly governs secretion by the lining. Sensory neurons in the wall detect stretch (mechanoreceptors) and chemistry of the contents (chemoreceptors); interneurons link the plexuses; motor neurons drive muscle and glands, so a local reflex can run entirely inside the wall. The autonomic nervous system tunes the ENS: parasympathetic fibres (mostly the vagus, plus pelvic nerves from the sacral cord for the last half of the colon) increase motility and secretion and relax sphincters; sympathetic fibres from the thoracolumbar cord do the opposite, which is why fear and anger slow digestion. The slide's figure is not Tortora's; Figure 24.4 gives the same wiring more abstractly.

basics: The abdominal organs are not loose in a bag; they are wrapped by the peritoneum, the body's largest serous membrane: a single layer of flat cells (mesothelium) on a thin connective-tissue backing. The part lining the abdominal wall is parietal; the part covering the organs is visceral (the same sheet as the gut's serosa). Between them is only a film of lubricating fluid, the peritoneal cavity. Because the membrane folds back on itself around the organs it forms double sheets that tether them and carry their vessels and nerves: the mesentery (jejunum and ileum), the mesocolons (transverse and sigmoid colon), the lesser omentum (stomach to liver), the greater omentum (a fat-laden apron hanging from the stomach over the intestines) and the falciform ligament (liver to anterior wall). Organs pressed against the back wall and covered on their front only (kidneys, pancreas, most of the duodenum, ascending and descending colon) are retroperitoneal. The slide's figure is Tortora Figure 24.5a.

basics: Saliva comes from hundreds of tiny glands in the lining plus three large paired glands outside it, each delivering through a duct. The parotid, in front of and below the ear, sends its duct across the cheek muscle to open opposite the upper second molar. The submandibular, under the floor of the mouth beside the jaw, opens either side of the lingual frenulum. The sublingual, under the tongue, opens by several small ducts onto the floor of the mouth. Together they make about 1-1.5 litres a day (the slide's 1.5 L is the upper figure). Saliva is 99.5% water with ions, mucus, antibacterial agents and salivary amylase; it dissolves food so it can be tasted and digested, lubricates the bolus and cleans the mouth. Parasympathetic nerves (VII and IX) keep a steady flow and boost it when food is tasted or smelled; sympathetic dominance (stress, dehydration) dries the mouth. The slide's figure is Tortora 24.7a.

basics: Under the microscope a salivary gland is a branching tree of ducts ending in bunches of secretory cells called acini (grape-like clusters). Two cell types line them. Serous cells are dark, pyramidal and packed with protein-making machinery; they release a watery fluid carrying amylase and electrolytes. Mucous cells look pale and foamy because they are full of mucin, which becomes slippery mucus. Some acini are purely serous, some purely mucous, and some mixed, where a cap of serous cells sits on a mucous acinus as a crescent, the serous demilune. The proportions differ by gland: parotid all serous, submandibular mostly serous with some mucous, sublingual mostly mucous. The ducts modify the fluid and carry it to the mouth; the supporting connective tissue between lobules is the stroma. Tortora shows only the submandibular micrograph (Figure 24.7b) and does not label demilunes, ducts or stroma; the caption gives the serous/mucous makeup of all three glands.

basics: Swallowing moves a bolus from mouth to stomach across a crossroads where the food route and the air route share the pharynx, so the airway must be sealed for a moment. Stage 1, voluntary: the tongue presses up and back against the palate and shoves the bolus into the oropharynx. That is the last thing under conscious control. Stage 2, pharyngeal (involuntary): receptors in the oropharynx signal the swallowing centre in the brain stem, which raises the soft palate and uvula to shut the nasopharynx, lifts the larynx so the epiglottis folds over its opening, briefly stops breathing, and relaxes the upper oesophageal sphincter so the bolus drops into the oesophagus. Stage 3, oesophageal, is peristalsis down the tube (next slide). The slide's drawing is Figure 24.11a-b. Unsaid: the whole sequence takes 4-8 s for solids, about 1 s for liquids, and the pharyngeal muscles are skeletal muscle acting reflexly.

basics: Peristalsis is how a muscular tube pushes a lump along: just behind the bolus the circular muscle contracts, narrowing the tube and squeezing the bolus forward; just ahead of it the longitudinal muscle contracts, shortening and widening that segment to receive it; the wave then moves on, repeating down the tube. When the wave reaches the bottom, the lower oesophageal sphincter relaxes and the bolus enters the stomach. Mucus from oesophageal glands lubricates the ride. The slide's arrangement 'outer longitudinal, inner circular' is the standard gut layout. It attributes the rhythm to the vagus nerve (parasympathetic), which is broadly right: the oesophageal wave is coordinated from the medulla via the vagus, and parasympathetic input raises motility throughout the gut. Unsaid: the upper third of the oesophagus is skeletal muscle, only the lower third is entirely smooth muscle, and peristalsis also occurs in ureters, bile ducts and uterine tubes.

terms.d: A travelling wave of contraction behind and relaxation ahead of the contents that propels them along a tube.

basics: The oesophagus is a 25 cm collapsible tube behind the trachea that pierces the diaphragm through the oesophageal hiatus to reach the stomach. Its wall follows the four-layer plan. The lining is nonkeratinised stratified squamous epithelium, many cells thick, because it must resist abrasion rather than absorb; under it lie lamina propria and muscularis mucosae. The submucosa contains mucus-secreting oesophageal glands whose ducts pierce the mucosa to lubricate the bolus, plus the submucosal plexus. The muscular layer is inner circular and outer longitudinal with the myenteric plexus (and its parasympathetic ganglia) between; it is skeletal muscle in the upper third and smooth in the lower third. The outermost layer in Tortora is an adventitia, loose connective tissue blending with the mediastinum, not a serosa, because the thoracic oesophagus has no serous covering; only the short abdominal segment does. basics: A negative feedback loop is a controller that senses a variable and acts to push it back toward a set point. Here the variables are the pH of the stomach contents and the stretch of the wall. When food arrives, the wall is distended and proteins buffer the acid, so pH rises: stretch receptors and chemoreceptors fire, the signals go to the submucosal plexus (the control centre), which activates parasympathetic and enteric motor neurons. The effectors respond: parietal cells secrete more HCl (pH falls back) and the wall muscle contracts harder (mixing waves and gastric emptying, so distension falls). Once pH is low and the stomach has emptied, the stimulus is gone and secretion stops. This is the neural part of the gastric phase; the hormonal part (gastrin) runs in parallel (slide 52). Tortora draws it as Figure 24.26. Unsaid: the cephalic phase (sight, smell, thought of food, via the vagus) has already primed secretion before food arrives.

basics: Four jobs. Mixing: waves of contraction sweep from body to antrum, pushing contents toward the closed pylorus (propulsion) and squirting them back (retropulsion) until the food becomes liquid chyme. Secretion of gastric juice: HCl kills microbes, unfolds (denatures) proteins and activates pepsinogen to pepsin; pepsin is the only stomach enzyme that cuts proteins; intrinsic factor is needed for later B12 absorption; gastric lipase attacks some fats. Endocrine secretion: G cells release gastrin into the blood to drive acid, pepsinogen and motility. Unsaid: the stomach absorbs little (some water, ions, alcohol, aspirin), and it protects itself by secreting pepsin in inactive form and by an alkaline mucus coat.

basics: Two kinds of muscular movement have been introduced. Peristalsis is a propulsive wave: circular muscle squeezes behind the contents, longitudinal muscle shortens the segment ahead, and the wave travels, moving material onward (oesophagus, stomach, and as the migrating motility complex in the intestine). Segmentation is a mixing movement: rings of circular muscle contract at intervals, chopping a distended segment into short lengths, then relax while new rings contract in between, so chyme sloshes back and forth without net progress; it happens 8-12 times a minute in the small intestine and brings chyme into contact with the wall. Chemical digestion so far: salivary amylase and lingual lipase in the mouth, pepsin and gastric lipase in the stomach; the pancreas and intestinal brush border will finish carbohydrates, proteins, lipids and nucleic acids. Tortora has no dedicated figure of segmentation vs peristalsis; the slide's drawing is the lecturer's.

basics: Absorption means getting a molecule from the lumen, across the absorptive cell, and out into the capillary or lacteal. Each nutrient class uses a transport mechanism matched to its chemistry. basics: Because all blood from the gut passes through it first, the liver is the body's chemical processing plant. Carbohydrate: it buffers blood glucose, storing it as glycogen after meals and releasing it (or making new glucose from amino acids and lactate) between them. Lipid: it burns fatty acids, makes cholesterol and lipoproteins, and turns cholesterol into bile salts. basics: The colon moves its contents slowly because its job is to absorb water and let bacteria work, so most of its movements mix rather than propel. Mass peristalsis is the exception: a few times a day, usually during or just after a meal (the gastrocolic reflex triggered by food entering the stomach), a strong wave starts around the middle of the transverse colon and sweeps the contents of descending and sigmoid colon into the rectum in one push, producing the urge to defecate. Entry from the ileum is likewise meal-timed: the gastroileal reflex intensifies ileal peristalsis and the partly closed ileal orifice lets chyme trickle into the caecum. Unsaid: contents spend 3-10 hours here, and reduced motility means more water absorbed and harder stools.
